discovery: Optical lattice atomic clocks reaching 10^-18 accuracy and their use as precision probes of fundamental physics

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / precision metrology
motivation: Katori proposed the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms are held in a lattice tuned to a 'magic' wavelength so that trapping leaves the clock transition unshifted. This brought the statistical power of many atoms to optical frequency standards without trap perturbation. Katori demonstrated the first lattice clocks and showed that cryogenic clocks compared over fiber links can measure gravitational redshift. Ye turned the concept into the world's most accurate clocks. He used frequency-comb-referenced ultrastable lasers, controlled quantum many-body interactions in degenerate Fermi gases, and resolved the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atomic sample. Together their work improved timekeeping by more than two orders of magnitude, to the 10^-18 level. It is driving the redefinition of the SI second and enables relativistic geodesy and searches for dark matter and varying constants. This is metrology-grade optics that changed what physics can measure.
